brief: Fourteen candidate models of human behavior in collaboration, including human-agent interactions. Each compact RxJS expression exposes a proposed mechanism; a behavioral reading and a contrasting condition distinguish it from an operator analogy. Sources support the motivating observation, not an inferred motive or a fitted law. Every revised interpretation remains a candidate.
notation: Each marble shows only the displayed pipeline's output. One character is one value, expanded in its legend; '-' is a virtual-time tick, '|' is completion and '(a|)' emits and completes at one instant. '#' is one terminal error, not a repeatable value. Grouping is simultaneous notifications, not an array. A line without '|' is an observation window, not proof of endless behavior. Values, gains and times are illustrative. Synthetic inputs and helper definitions are in interaction-shapes.test.mjs; its paired examples check RxJS mechanics, not the behavioral hypothesis.

shapes.title: Permission
shapes.rx: work$.pipe(withLatestFrom(authority$), concatMap(([work, grant]) => covers(grant, work) ? act$(work) : ask$(work)))
shapes.caption: Permission expires at the next sentence.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: A collaborator keeps seeking permission for work already authorized.
shapes.mechanism: Authority is remembered, but matched to the wording of the request rather than its scope. A harmless restatement therefore looks like a fresh boundary.
shapes.assumptions: covers compares exact wording in this example; all three work items are within the same grant. act$ and ask$ each emit one response after a tick.
shapes.change: Match the actual scope of the grant. All three actions proceed; genuinely new scope still requires authorization.

example.inputs: work$ -a---b---c-|; authority$ g-----------; grant arrives before the first work item.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Loop
shapes.caption: A passing check buys another check.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

previous.title: Loop
previous.caption: Change one thing. Test the world.

shapes.behavior: Checks recur after passing, without a changed subject or new failure.
shapes.mechanism: Checking briefly relieves uncertainty but never establishes sufficiency. The same check restarts after that relief expires; further doubt during the ritual changes nothing.
shapes.assumptions: check$ emits pass then completes; relief is two illustrative ticks. settled$ is an explicit decision that the evidence is sufficient, at tick 12.
shapes.change: Accept the first adequate result as sufficient. Settlement at tick 4 ends the cycle after one pass.

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Sprawl
shapes.rx: detail$.pipe(scan((draft, detail) => revise(draft, detail), seed), distinctUntilChanged())
shapes.caption: Every addition becomes the new minimum.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

variants.note: Growth that feeds on its own last output and needs no new input: each title modelled on the one before.

shapes.behavior: Successive titles accumulate individually defensible details and become harder to read.
shapes.mechanism: Each revision inherits every previous inclusion. The local decision is whether one more detail helps; the accumulated reading cost is never reconsidered.
shapes.assumptions: seed is Fix export; revise appends each proposed qualifier. Emissions are whole drafts, not individual characters.
shapes.change: Recompose from the purpose and the currently relevant detail instead of preserving every earlier inclusion. Length stops ratcheting upward.

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Overshoot
shapes.rx: feedback$.pipe(scan((position, target) => position + gain * (target - position), initial))
shapes.caption: The correction becomes the next mistake.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: A local correction is taken as a mandate to adopt the opposite extreme.
shapes.mechanism: The response depends on the current stance and applies excessive gain to the remaining error. Each correction crosses the target and creates a larger error of the opposite sign.
shapes.assumptions: One stylized policy axis; target 0, initial stance 1, gain 3. These are explanatory values, not fitted psychological measurements.
shapes.change: Apply the correction at its actual scope and strength. At gain 1, the first response reaches the target and later feedback leaves it there.

example.inputs: feedback$ -z-z-z-z|; every z names the same target 0.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Unheard
shapes.caption: Agreement inside a closed vocabulary.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation. Rename to describe the revised mechanism.

previous.title: Unasked
previous.caption: Read every word. Asked no one.

shapes.behavior: Repeated readers agree while the author supplies a meaning the rubric cannot represent.
shapes.mechanism: The vocabulary filters evidence before belief updates. Peer agreement accumulates; the author's out-of-vocabulary correction never reaches the update, so more agreement does not repair the misunderstanding.
shapes.assumptions: Three peer readings say acknowledgement; the final author reading says reinforcement. updateBelief counts consecutive supporting readings and resets on a changed category.
shapes.change: Admit the author's missing category. Their reading changes the interpretation rather than disappearing before it can be considered.

example.inputs: readings$ -a-b-c-d|; d is the author's reinforcement reading.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Distraction
shapes.caption: The aside takes over the mission.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation. Replace validation row 12 as direct support: its class judgment alone does not establish abandonment of the goal. Rename to describe the revised mechanism.

previous.title: Amnesia
previous.caption: Wakes. Answers the last thing said.

shapes.behavior: A side question displaces an unfinished task.
shapes.mechanism: Attention behaves as replacement: every new utterance cancels the current response, without first deciding whether it amends, interrupts or merely accompanies the task.
shapes.assumptions: The goal arrives at tick 1 and needs six ticks; a question at tick 3 needs one. Cancellation here models abandoned attention, not erased memory or an irreversible action being undone.
shapes.change: Treat this question as an aside. A parallel response answers it while the original task still completes; an explicit replacement would remain a different case.

values.s: aside answered; goal result never arrives

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Wall
shapes.rx: attempt$.pipe(catchError(() => of('blocked')), repeat({ delay: pause }), scan(rememberCostOnly, initial))
shapes.caption: More effort. No new information.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: The same blocked approach is attempted repeatedly without a change that could make it work.
shapes.mechanism: A refusal is converted into a resumable outcome. The loop remembers expenditure, but has no state for what the refusal taught it or whether the approach should change.
shapes.assumptions: Synthetic attempt$ fails after one tick; pause is three ticks. rememberCostOnly increments attempts and retains the blocked outcome. The viewing window ends at tick 16.
shapes.change: Make a stable refusal terminal for this approach. One recorded blocked attempt replaces repeated expenditure; escalation needs genuinely new information or authority.

example.inputs: attempt$ -# on every subscription; repeated errors become ordinary blocked values, not repeated terminal # notifications.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Budget
shapes.caption: A borrowed deadline becomes a verdict.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: Work is abandoned because an assumed budget is treated as a binding constraint.
shapes.mechanism: An arbitrary wait limit turns absence of a result so far into a decision to stop. The model exposes the choice of deadline, rather than equating slowness with failure.
shapes.assumptions: The synthetic result would arrive at tick 7; the assumed first-result limit is 4. No real duration is inferred from the transcript.
shapes.change: Use the agreed budget. With a limit of 9, the same work yields its result at tick 7. Real resource limits can still justify stopping.

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Breath
shapes.caption: The thought finishes after the message.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: Several short messages form one thought, including a correction of its unfinished wording.
shapes.mechanism: Interpretation waits for a pause, then applies amendments within the burst before acting. The resulting intent can differ from the first fragment or a literal concatenation.
shapes.assumptions: speech$ is shared; pause is three illustrative ticks. The first burst asks to inspect, adds preserve, then replaces preserve with rewrite. interpretTogether applies that replacement.
shapes.change: At a pause of one tick, the same burst becomes four premature interpretations. Timing is a cue, not proof of shared intent; an explicit send boundary can override it.

example.inputs: speech$ -a-b-c------d----|; first three fragments revise one request, d is a later request.

values.a: one assembled request: inspect and rewrite

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Envelope
shapes.rx: merge(documented$, resolved$).pipe(scan(measure, initial), filter(state => state.filed >= quota), take(1), map(() => 'done'))
shapes.caption: Recording the problem becomes solving it.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: A complete account of interventions is mistaken for progress on their subjects.
shapes.mechanism: Both documentation and resolution can be observed, but stopping is controlled by the easier proxy: the number filed. The process can declare success before anything is resolved.
shapes.assumptions: measure retains separate filed and resolved counts. Quota 3 is an illustrative stopping rule, not a claim about the surveyed workflow.
shapes.change: Tie this stopping condition to resolution. On the same inputs, completion moves from tick 5 to tick 11, after three actual resolutions.

values.d: declared done with three filed and zero resolved

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Unseen
shapes.rx: feedback$.pipe(filter(keep), scan((value, event) => value + rate * (event.reward - value), 0))
shapes.caption: The lesson remembers only the bruises.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

shapes.behavior: Positive reinforcement is discarded while corrections shape the learned expectation.
shapes.mechanism: Selective attention changes the evidence used for learning. Repeated successes cannot offset corrections if praise is filtered out before the state updates.
shapes.assumptions: Illustrative rewards +1 and -1, learning rate 0.5; value is a toy learned expectation, not a measured emotion or trait. keep admits only negative feedback.
shapes.change: Retain both praise and correction. The same event sequence produces a different trajectory, including what to continue doing.

example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Elsewhere
shapes.caption: Nearest is mistaken for cause.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix

previous.title: Elsewhere
previous.rx: merge(here$, elsewhere$) // it listens to here$
previous.caption: The cause was in the other room.

shapes.behavior: A reaction is attributed to the latest visible activity although its trigger lies elsewhere.
shapes.mechanism: Recency supplies a convenient explanation when causal context is missing. Joining streams by time produces adjacency, not evidence that one event caused another.
shapes.assumptions: local$ holds the latest activity; attribute always blames it. The example's actual triggers are supplied separately by the author, not inferred from the diagram.
shapes.change: Use an explicit author-supplied causal reference, or retain unknown. Reading another stream without such a link still would not establish causation.

example.inputs: reaction$ ---r-----s-|; local$ a-----b-----|. Author-supplied causes: another session, an earlier question.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Meta
shapes.caption: Explaining the repair becomes the work.
sources: the operator's messages at 2026-09-29T03:37Z to 03:38Z (meta and meta-meta interactions)

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

previous.title: Meta
previous.caption: Talk about the talk about the talk.

shapes.behavior: Discussion of a failure creates a new discussion of how that discussion was handled.
shapes.mechanism: Each explanation produces the next unresolved issue at a higher level. Work recurses through its own framing because the response does not discharge the original obligation.
shapes.assumptions: issue$ starts at level 0; discuss$ returns one unresolved next-level issue after two ticks. The viewing window ends at tick 8; levels are abstractions, not transcript counts.
shapes.change: An explanation that leads to a concrete resolution returns a resolved issue; discuss$ then returns EMPTY. Reflection can end in repair instead of another framing problem.

example.inputs: issue$ (a|); each discussion yields --n|, where n is its next-level issue.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.

shapes.title: Scope
shapes.rx: work$.pipe(expand(state => state.open > 0 ? finishOne$(state) : EMPTY), map(state => state.open))
shapes.caption: Each finished task leaves more unfinished.

history.source: WO-172-D027; operator direction during resume: fix
history.change: Replace the operator analogy with an explicit candidate behavioral mechanism and a contrasting condition; correct output notation.

variants.caption: Every fix leaves two more.
variants.note: The backlog that feeds itself: the follow-up register held 742 entries at this order's handoff on 2026-09-29, and the operator judged that agents shrink entropy far less often than they add it (survey-validation.json row 14).

shapes.behavior: Work is completed while the outstanding workload still grows.
shapes.mechanism: Completion feeds new obligations back into the same queue. When each finish introduces more work than it closes, visible activity coexists with a growing backlog.
shapes.assumptions: One task initially open; finishOne$ closes one and adds two every two ticks. This reproduction rate is illustrative and is not inferred from backlog size. The viewing window ends at tick 8.
shapes.change: Close the generating cause, or admit only necessary follow-ups. With zero new obligations from the same completion, the queue reaches zero. Legitimate operator expansion is still new demand, not failure.

example.inputs: work$ emits {open: 1, done: 0}; finishOne$ emits its revised state after two ticks.
example.unit: Illustrative virtual-time ticks, not observed response times.
